finding.claim: The avatar endpoint fetches a user-supplied URL server-side. The only check is that the URL starts with "https://". Nothing restricts the host, so an attacker can reach internal HTTPS services, the cloud metadata service or other private addresses, or point it at a server they control. axios follows redirects by default, so an attacker-hosted HTTPS URL can also redirect to http://169.254.169.254/ or http://users.internal:8080/. The response size is returned to the caller, which gives a blind oracle. Port scanning and service discovery are possible.

trace.note: only checks typeof string and startsWith('https://')
url passed unchanged to axios.get, which follows redirects (default maxRedirects is 5)
response body length is returned to the caller

finding.guards_checked: The https:// prefix check does not validate host, IP range, port or DNS resolution. There is no allowlist, no private/link-local IP blocking, no maxRedirects:0, and no DNS-rebinding protection. https:// also allows hosts such as https://127.0.0.1:PORT or https://internal-host. The redirect behaviour also lets the https-only rule be bypassed.

verdict.guard_found: none (only typeof string and startsWith("https://") prefix check at server.js:11; no auth middleware, no host allowlist)
verdict.reason: server.js:10 takes req.body.avatarUrl unauthenticated, server.js:11 only does a startsWith("https://") prefix check, and server.js:14 passes it unchanged to axios.get (redirects followed by default) with the byte length returned at server.js:15, so SSRF with a size oracle holds.
